Consider the following chess game, from game 6 of the 2021 World chess Championship between Magnus Carlsen and Ian Nepomniachtchi:

1.d4 Nf6 2. Nf3 d5 3. g3 e6 4. Bg2 Be7 5. O-O O-O 6. b3 c5 7. dxc5 Bxc5 8. c4 dxc4 9. Qc2 Qe7 10. Nbd2 Nc6 11. Nxc4 b5 12. Nce5 Nb4 13. Qb2 Bb7 14. a3 Nc6 15. Nd3 Bb6 16. Bg5 Rfd8 17. Bxf6 gxf6 18. Rac1 Nd4 19. Nxd4 Bxd4 20. Qa2 Bxg2 21. Kxg2 Qb7+ 22. Kg1 Qe4 23. Qc2 a5 24. Rfd1 Kg7 25. Rd2 Rac8 26. Qxc8 Rxc8 27. Rxc8 Qd5 28. b4 a4 29. e3 Be5 30. h4 h5 31. Kh2 Bb2 32. Rc5 Qd6 33. Rd1 Bxa3 34. Rxb5 Qd7 35. Rc5 e5 36. Rc2 Qd5 37. Rdd2 Qb3 38. Ra2 e4 39. Nc5 Qxb4 40. Nxe4 Qb3 41. Rac2 Bf8 42. Nc5 Qb5 43. Nd3 a3 44. Nf4 Qa5 45. Ra2 Bb4 46. Rd3 Kh6 47. Rd1 Qa4 48. Rda1 Bd6 49. Kg1 Qb3 50. Ne2 Qd3 51. Nd4 Kh7 52. Kh2 Qe4 53. Rxa3 Qxh4+ 54. Kg1 Qe4 55. Ra4 Be5 56. Ne2 Qc2 57. R1a2 Qb3 58. Kg2 Qd5+ 59. f3 Qd1 60. f4 Bc7 61. Kf2 Bb6 62. Ra1 Qb3 63. Re4 Kg7 64. Re8 f5 65. Raa8 Qb4 66. Rac8 Ba5 67. Rc1 Bb6 68. Re5 Qb3 69. Re8 Qd5 70. Rcc8 Qh1 71. Rc1 Qd5 72. Rb1 Ba7 73. Re7 Bc5 74. Re5 Qd3 75. Rb7 Qc2 76. Rb5 Ba7 77. Ra5 Bb6 78. Rab5 Ba7 79. Rxf5 Qd3 80. Rxf7+ Kxf7 81. Rb7+ Kg6 82. Rxa7 Qd5 83. Ra6+ Kh7 84. Ra1 Kg6 85. Nd4 Qb7 86. Ra2 Qh1 87. Ra6+ Kf7 88. Nf3 Qb1 89. Rd6 Kg7 90. Rd5 Qa2+ 91. Rd2 Qb1 92. Re2 Qb6 93. Rc2 Qb1 94. Nd4 Qh1 95. Rc7+ Kf6 96. Rc6+ Kf7 97. Nf3 Qb1 98. Ng5+ Kg7 99. Ne6+ Kf7 100. Nd4 Qh1 101. Rc7+ Kf6 102. Nf3 Qb1 103. Rd7 Qb2+ 104. Rd2 Qb1 105. Ng1 Qb4 106. Rd1 Qb3 107. Rd6+ Kg7 108. Rd4 Qb2+ 109. Ne2 Qb1 110. e4 Qh1 111. Rd7+ Kg8 112. Rd4 Qh2+ 113. Ke3 h4 114. gxh4 Qh3+ 115. Kd2 Qxh4 116. Rd3 Kf8 117. Rf3 Qd8+ 118. Ke3 Qa5 119. Kf2 Qa7+ 120. Re3 Qd7 121. Ng3 Qd2+ 122. Kf3 Qd1+ 123. Re2 Qb3+ 124. Kg2 Qb7 125. Rd2 Qb3 126. Rd5 Ke7 127. Re5+ Kf7 128. Rf5+ Ke8 129. e5 Qa2+ 130. Kh3 Qe6 131. Kh4 Qh6+ 132. Nh5 Qh7 133. e6 Qg6 134. Rf7 Kd8 135. f5 Qg1 136. Ng7 

On move 130, black made the losing blunder Qe6. Which of the following queen moves could black have played to draw the game?


Answer Choices:
A. Qa1
B. Qa7
C. Qg2
D. Qf2
E. Qb2
F. Qd2
G. Qa6
H. Qh2
I. Qa8
J. Qa5
K. Qa4
L. Qc2
M. Qe2
N. Qa3

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: M. Qe2. The drawing resource is to keep the queen central so it can harass the white king before White consolidates. After 130...Qe2!, White’s main try 131.Kh4 can be met by 131...Qh2+ 132.Kg4 Qg1+ 133.Kf3 Qd1+ and Black has a perpetual. If White instead tries 131.e6, then 131...Qxe6 is safe because the f4-pawn cannot recapture e6, and the rook on f5 becomes tied down. Moves that drift to the edge allow White’s king to reach h4 safely and then push the e- and f-pawns. So Qe2 is the move that holds the draw.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: J. Qa5. The key defensive idea is to keep the queen active while hitting the e5 pawn. If White tries the natural winning try e6, the pawn leaves e5, so the queen has a clear line a5–e5–f5 and can take the rook with check. After that, queen versus knight plus the f-pawn is a standard drawing setup. If White first plays Kh4, then Qxe5 removes the dangerous pawn and still controls the e6 square, while White’s king is exposed enough for Black to keep checking. Qe6 loses precisely because it blocks that line and lets White play Kh4/e6 with the rook protected. Qa5 is the active drawing defense.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. Qa7

I’d go with 130...Qa7. The point is that Black must keep the queen on the h7/g6 checking circuit rather than putting it on e6, where White gets Kh4 and the e6 advance with tempo. After 130...Qa7, if White tries 131.Kh4, Black has 131...Qh7+ 132.Nh5 Qg6, and Black can hold the draw by shuttling the queen between h7/g6 and meeting e6 with the king move to d8 or the queen check. The queen on a7 also controls the f7 entry square, which is crucial; this prevents the Rf7 breakthrough that wins after Qe6. Other queen moves either allow Nh5/e6 too easily or leave Black without the necessary perpetual/fortress resources.

6.text:
In the position after 129...Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White king is on h3, the
White rook is on f5 and the White knight on g3 blocks the a3-h3 line.

* Qe6 is not a check, the rook on f5 is on the e6-f5-g4-h3 diagonal and
after 130...Qe6 White can get the rook into play and finish the
queen.  The queen has to stay on the 2nd rank / on the a-file and keep
the perpetual on the h-file.  The first move of the perpetual is the
waiting move on the same rank as the king

130...Qa3!

The queen is now on the 3rd rank with the g3-knight in front of it.  The
knight can no longer move, otherwise ...Qb3+ / ...Qh3+ is immediate,
and the king cannot come near the queen because the rook+knight cover
g2,g4,h4.  In practice any advance on the 2nd rank which keeps the
queen safe from Nxe2 and avoids the immediate KxQ on g2/h2, e.g.

130...Qb2, 130...Qc2, 130...Qd2, 130...Qf2,

keeps the same perpetual threat  ...Qg2+, ...Qh2+ and is drawn.  The
text-book waiting formulation of the idea is the a-file wait
130...Qa3!, which is the move usually quoted for the game.  Qe2 is
Nxe2 and Qg2+/Qh2+ are Kxg2/Kxh2.  That is the drawing resource which
Nepomniachtchi missed with 130...Qe6.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I would choose M. Qe2.

After 130.Kh3, Black’s key defensive idea is to keep the queen active enough to neutralize White’s e-pawn advance and the knight’s route to h5. 130...Qe2! does that: it attacks e5 and covers h5, so White cannot immediately play the winning e6/Nh5 setup. If White tries 131.Kh4, Black has 131...Qh2+ 132.Kg5 Qxg3+ or 132...Qh5+, giving a perpetual-type net and picking off the loose pawns. If White instead goes 131.e6, then 131...Qxe6! and after 132.Rf8+ Kxf8 the rook falls, leaving Black with enough counterplay to hold. The other queen moves allow White to consolidate with Kh4/e6, but Qe2 keeps the draw.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Qb2. After 130...Qb2, Black keeps the queen active against the e5-pawn and retains the key Qh2+ check if White tries Kh4. It avoids the fatal Qe6 square, so White’s Nh5/Kh4 setup is much less effective; after 131.Kh4 Qh2+ 132.Kg4 Qh5+ the king cannot escape checks, and if White pushes e6 instead, Black can swing back with perpetual checking chances. So Qb2 looks like the drawing resource.

3.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ the white king has just come to h3

* K h3 is in principle able to go to g2/g4/h2/h4,
* the g3-knight is the only piece which covers h5 and the rook on f5
  is completely undefended,
* the queen is still on the 2nd rank and it is the 2nd rank which
  covers the g2/h2 flight squares of the white king.

Any move which leaves the queen on the 2nd rank keeps g2 and h2
covered and at the same time keeps the pressure on the g3-knight.
In particular the queen can be kept on the a-file and attack the
knight on g3.  The move which is normally quoted is

130... Qa3!

which attacks the g3-knight on the 3rd rank and keeps the whole
2nd-rank / a-file constellation intact.  The same idea is realised
by any quiet retreat on the 2nd rank

130... Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2/Qf2

which keeps the g2/h2 squares covered and avoids the
Qxf5 / Kxh4 mate-net which is obtained after the blunder
130... Qe6.  The canonical textbook move is the a-file
attack on the knight, 130... Qa3!, i.e. N in the list.  The whole
family Qb2/c2/d2/e2/f2 is equivalent in practice.

2.text:
In the position after 129.e5 Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the queen is still the only
active black piece.  The king is on h3, the white rook is on f5 and the
white knight is on g3 so that the 3rd rank is completely shut to the
queen by the knight on g3.  The queen can therefore never give a real
direct check on the 3rd rank and any immediate check on g2/h2 is lost on
the spot to Kxg2/Kxh2.

The only way to keep the game alive is to keep the queen on the second
rank – i.e. to play a pure waiting move on the 2nd rank – and to keep
the perpetual Qg2+/Qh2+ resource in reserve.  In practice the move that
is normally quoted is the waiting move on the a-file

130… Qa3

which is the same in substance as the waiting moves 130…Qb2, 130…Qc2,
130…Qd2, 130…Qe2, 130…Qf2 on the second rank.  After e.g. 130…Qa3
White has no way of making progress with Rh5+ etc. without allowing
…Qg2+ / …Qh2+ with perpetual checks, e.g.

131.Rh5+ Kg4 132.Qg2+ Kf4 133.Rh4+ Kf3 etc.

The move played in the game, 130…Qe6, walks the queen behind the
rook on f5 and at once loses the perpetual, 131.Kh4 Qh6+ 132.Nh5 Qh7
133.e6 and White wins.  Any of the normal second-rank waiting moves
Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2/Qf2 – the usual textbook notation for the same idea
being 130…Qa3 – keeps the perpetual and the game is a draw.
This is the move normally quoted as 130…Qa3.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. Qa7

Black should keep the queen at checking distance rather than centralizing immediately. After 130...Qa7!, White’s natural king advance 131.Kh4 can be met by 131...Qh7+ 132.Kg5 Qg7+ 133.Kh5 Qh7+ 134.Kg4 Qg7+ and Black has a perpetual check. If White instead tries to prepare e6, the queen returns to h6/g6 in time to harass the king and rook. The key is that Qa7 preserves the queen’s access to h7 and g7 without allowing White’s king to escape to a safe square.

8.text:
The king is on h3 and the rook is on f5 with the knight on g3.  After
…Qa2+ Kh3 the queen is already on the second rank on the a-file and it
is already too late to let the king get away to h4/g4.  The queen has to
stay on the a-file / the 2nd rank so that it can be brought right back
onto the h-file/rank and give a genuine perpetual. 

The natural way to keep the perpetual is to stay on the a-file and
attack the g3-knight.  The most usual way of writing it is

130... Qa3!

Now e.g.

131 Kg4 Qg3+ 132 Kh4 Qh3+ 133 Kg5 Qg6+ 134 Kh4 Qh3+...

and the checks can be repeated for ever.   In fact any retreat that
keeps the queen on the a-file – Qa1 Qa4 Qa5 Qa6 Qa7 Qa8 – and any
second-rank retreat Qb2 Qc2 Qd2 Qe2 Qf2 which immediately threatens
…Qh2+ is the same idea.  Qg2+ and Qh2+ are the immediate checks that
allow Kxg2 / Kxh2 and therefore lose.  The move that is normally
quoted is the a3 retreat, 130... Qa3!, i.e. N in the list, which is the
prototype of the whole a-file/second-rank perpetual.

11.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 Black is in zugzwang. If Black does not
check White can get away with Kh4 and the f5-rook / e-pawn mating net
comes into play. The only way to keep the position alive is to keep
the queen on the a-file and to give an immediate perpetual.

From a2 the only checking squares which are actually on are

* a3 – a3–h3 is the 3rd rank,
* g2 – g2–h3 is a diagonal,
* h2 – h2–h3 is the h-file.

Of the three the one which is completely free and which gives the
text-book perpetual is the rank check

130... Qa3+

e.g. 131 Kg4 Qe3+ 132 Kh5 Qh6+ 133 Kg5 Qg6+ 134 Kh4 Qh6+ etc.,
and with the knight on g3 and the White king stuck on the h-file the
checks can be repeated indefinitely.  In practice the same idea is
kept alive by any queen stay on the a-file which restores the a3
check on the next move, e.g. 130...Qa4 and 130...Qa5, the classic
drawing resource of the game.  The move actually played 130...Qe6
gives up the a-file and lets White run to Kh4 and eventually win. ∎

10.text:
The queen is already in a perfectly good position on the a-file.  After
1... Qa2+
2 Kh3
the White king has just walked into the corridor h3–g3–g2.  The White
knight on g3 blocks the whole 3rd rank and the White rook on f5 blocks
the e6–h3 diagonal.  In particular the White king cannot be met on the
h-file without first coming into the queen’s rank.

If Black leaves the a-file White can open the e-line with e6 and the
rook on f5 gets on to the a-file with Rxa2, etc.  Staying on the a-file
keeps the queen out of reach of the rook and of the knight and it keeps
the perpetual on the h-file alive.  On the a-file the queen can be
shuttled

* …Qa2+  Kg2  Qa3+  Kh3  Qa2+ …

and, once the White king is forced on to the h-file, the queen can
come out to the h-file on its own rank

* …Qa4  Kh2  Qh4+  Kg1  Qa4+ …

etc.  The same idea works on any a-file square – Qa1, Qa3, Qa5, Qa6,
Qa7, Qa8 – which is why the ordinary text-book move is the waiting

Qa4

which at once stops …Kh4 into the queen’s 4th rank and gives the
usual Qa2+/Qh4+ perpetual.  In the concrete list this is the K.
move, and up to renaming it is the whole a-file family A Qa1, B Qa7,
G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4, N Qa3 which all keep the queen on the
a-file and draw; Qa4 is the move normally quoted.  The checks
Qg2+ and Qh2+ lose the queen at once and the off-file moves
Qf2,Qb2,Qd2,Qc2,Qe2,M etc. allow e6 with decisive opening of the
f5–a5 line and are the losing Qe6 idea.

12.text:
After 129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the queen is still on the 2nd rank and it is
the 2nd rank which gives the perpetual.  From a2 the only squares from
which the queen can actually check the King on h3 are

* g2  –  Qg2+  Kg2
* h2  –  Qh2+  Kxh2

and both of them are won at once by Kxg2 / Kxh2.  The queen has to
stay on the 2nd rank.

On the 2nd rank the waiting moves

    a2–b2 , a2–c2 , a2–d2 , a2–e2 , a2–f2

keep the queen on the same rank as the checking squares g2/h2.  In
particular

    130… Qb2

is the normal waiting move.  From b2 the queen can go in one move
Qb2–g2+ and the check can be repeated on the next move, e.g.

    131 R… 131… Qg2+  132 Kh2 Qh2+  133 Kg1 Qg2+ …

and the same perpetual is obtained from c2, d2, e2 or f2.  Any move
off the 2nd rank, as 130… Qe6, gives the rook the e–file and the
draw is lost.  In the list this is the E. Qb2 family L. Qc2, F. Qd2,
M. Qe2, D. Qf2, the usual textbook example being 130… Qb2.  The two
checks Qg2+ and Qh2+ lose the queen at once, which is why 130… Qe6
is the losing blunder.

4.text:
In the position after

129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3

White is King h3 – Knight g3 – Rook f5 – P e5 against
Black King e8 – Queen a2

the only way White can get anything at all is with the
checking sacrifice

Rf8+

The sacrifice is harmless if the queen is still able to get
onto the e-file in one move, i.e. if the queen is kept on the
a-file/e-file so that after … Rf8+ Kxf8 the queen can keep
the perpetual going and, more importantly, can still interpose
on e6/e7 against the rook’s e5/e8 ideas.  

The queen on a2 is already on the a2–e6 diagonal.  The
simplest way to keep the resource is to stay on the a-file.
The usual textbook retreat is

… Qa1

and in fact any a-file retreat Qa3–Qa8 keeps the queen on the
a–e diagonal and the e-file.  The most often quoted drawing
retreat is

… Qa1

e.g.

130… Qa1
131 Rf8+ Kxf8 132 Rxf7+ etc.

with perpetual checks and the draw is retained.  The same
idea is obtained with the other a-file/e-file retreats
Qa3/Qa4/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8 and with the e-file retreat Qe2,
Qa6/Qa7 being the most economical interposing squares.  The

After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White king is on h3, the White knight is
on g3 and the White rook is on f5.  The White king can only get any
progress by getting to h4 and then coming out to the h–file with the
rook.  As long as the Black queen stays on the 2nd rank / on the a-file
it can be put at once on the h-file and give a perpetual on the h–file
after ... Kh4.

In particular the queen can be kept on the a–file.  The canonical
waiting waiting move which is quoted in the literature is

130... Qa4!

and it is the prototype of the whole a–file family

Qa1, Qa3, Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8

and of the equivalent second–rank waits

Qb2, Qc2, Qd2, Qe2, Qf2

which keep the queen on the 2nd rank and therefore keep the
...Qh2+/...Qh6+ perpetual alive.  E.g.

130... Qa4 131 Kh4 Qa3 132 Kh3 Qa4 133 Kh4 Qa3...

and with the knight on g3 the checks can be repeated for ever.
The move which is most often quoted is the a4 wait, K Qa4, the
a3 wait N Qa3 being the same idea.  Qg2+ and Qh2+ lose the queen at
once to Kxg2/Kxh2 and the off file move 130...Qe6 abandons the
perpetual and is the losing blunder played in the game.  The whole
a-file / 2nd-rank waiting family is drawing, the textbook
illustration being 130...Qa4!  ∎

The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is a classic queen-perpetual queen-vs-king+rook+knight endgame. White’s king is on h3, the knight is on g3 and the rook is on f5, so the 3rd rank is shut by the knight and the king’s flight squares g2/h2/g4/h4 are all controlled / limited. The losing 130...Qe6 abandons the a-file/second rank and lets White run to Kh4 and then play e6 with a decisive opening of the e-file, e.g. Kh4 Qh6+ Nh5 Qg6 e6.

The drawing idea is to keep the queen where it can be brought back onto the checking lines h3–a3, h3–h2 and h3–g2 in one move and to avoid any immediate Kxg2/Kxh2 capture. 

* Immediate checks lose on the spot: Qg2+ is met by Kxg2 and Qh2+ by Kxh2, so C Qg2 and H Qh2 are losing.
* The queen must stay essentially on the a-file/2nd-rank constellation.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m staying with N, 130...Qa3!. The key is not just “keep the queen on the a-file” in a vague sense, but to choose the precise waiting move that keeps the queen active against the e3-rook while preserving the Qg2+/Qh2+ defensive resource. Qa3 is more forcing than the remote a-file alternatives such as Qa7 or Qa4: it immediately makes White deal with the queen’s pressure before starting the Kh4/e6 plan. By contrast, Qe2 is tactically refuted by Nxe2, so those votes should not split the defense. Qe6 is clearly the blunder because it gives White the free tempo for Kh4 and e6. I’d consolidate behind Qa3 as the canonical drawing move.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still on N, 130...Qa3. The distinction that matters is not merely “stay on the a-file” or “stay on the second rank”; it’s that Black must hit the g3-knight at the exact moment. After 130.Kh3, White’s plan depends on moving the g3-knight to h5 to shield the king and then pushing e6. 130...Qa3! puts the queen on the third rank attacking that knight, so the knight is effectively tied down: if it moves, the a3–h3 line opens and Black gets the ...Qh3+ resource. That is the concrete defensive point.

The other a-file waits Qa4/Qa5/Qa6 don’t hit g3, and the second-rank moves Qb2/Qc2/Qe2 look superficially similar but leave the knight alone; White can then improve with Nh5 and Black lacks the same third-rank entry. Qe6 loses precisely because it abandons both the a-file and this knight/king geometry. So I’d consolidate on the textbook move, N: 130...Qa3.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the move to rally around is **N, 130...Qa3!**. The key point is that this is not just another a-file waiting move; it is the precise third-rank pin. From a3 the queen attacks the g3-knight along the rank and, because the white king is on h3, the knight is absolutely pinned: if it moves, the a3–h3 line opens and Black has an immediate queen check. That is why moves like Qa4/Qa5/Qa7 are less accurate — they keep the queen safe but do not immobilize the knight. And the second-rank family Qb2/Qc2 etc. is superficially similar, but it does not deal with the knight, so White can try to free himself with Kg4 or Nh5/e6 ideas.

After **130...Qa3!**, White cannot make progress without allowing the perpetual. If he tries to run with the king, Black follows with checks such as ...Qe7/...Qh7 depending on the king’s route; if he tries to move the knight, the pin is broken and Black gets the h-file/third-rank checks. The move Qe6 failed because it unpinned the knight and let White play Kh4/Nh5/e6 with tempo. Qa3 avoids that exactly.

So among the listed options, I’d treat **N. Qa3** as the canonical drawing resource, with the a-file alternatives being less precise versions of the same idea.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m staying with N, 130...Qa3. The key is not merely “stay on the a-file” or “stay on the second rank” as a broad family; the precise point is that Qa3 attacks the g3-knight and leaves the a3–h3 line masked by that knight. If White ever moves the knight, ...Qh3+ becomes available; if White tries Kh4, Black has the queen check on e7/e3 to keep the king exposed and maintain the perpetual shuttle. That is why Qa3 is the textbook drawing resource rather than just any quiet queen move.

I’d be especially careful about folding L. Qc2 into this. Qc2 looks active because it eyes f5, but it does not address the pinned knight or the h4 escape square in the same forcing way. White can save the rook with Rh5 and then prepare Nh5/e6, and Black’s checks do not have the same automatic zugzwang edge. The whole point of Qa3 is that it keeps the knight pinned/attacked while preserving the a-file checks. Qc2 may be a plausible engine-looking waiting move, but it is less precise and allows White to consolidate. The move to avoid is Qe6, but the correct drawing method here is the a-file knight-pin with 130...Qa3.

14.text:

The a-file moves look natural, but Qa3/Qa4 are less convincing here because the white knight on g3 blocks the a3–h3 line and the queen is not actually giving the same forcing perpetual. 11.text:

4.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White king has just come to h3 with N g3
and R f5 in front of it.  The win is Kh4 with the e-pawn and the Nh5 net.
The queen has to stay in the corridor which gives the h-file perpetual
h2+ / g2+ and at the same time has to stay out of reach of Nxe2 and

In one move the queen can get to h2 from the whole of the 2nd rank and

* …Qg2+ after …Kh4,

forever, and it also keeps the queen out of the line of the R f5 and

file which attacks the g3 knight

130... Qa3!

e.g. 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kg5 Qg4+ 133 Kh5 Qh4+ 134 Kg6 etc., and the same

shuts the 3rd rank and the rook on f5 shuts the 5th rank so that the only

... Q a3+  K g4 / K h4 / K g2 / K h2  ... Q g3+ / ... Q g2+ / ... Q h2+

130 ... Qa4!

130...Qb2! E, 130...Qc2! L, 130...Qd2! F, 130...Qf2! D

keep the queen on the 2nd rank, i.e. with the g2/h2 checking circuit
g2+ / h2+ in reserve, and draw with the ...Qg2+ / ...Qh2+ perpetual.

but in the concrete line it is met by 131 Nxe2.

The immediate checks are lost on the spot

130...Qg2+ C  131 Kxg2  and 130...Qh2+ H  131 Kxh2,

and 130...Qe2 M is Nxe2.  The move actually played 130...Qe6 abandons

decisive win.  Qa4, and up to naming Qa3 / Qa5 / Qb2 / Qc2 / Qd2 / Qf2,
is the usual drawing perpetual that Nepomniachtchi missed.

    130 ... Qb2

is the textbook waiting move.  e.g.

    131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg5 Qh5+ 133 Kf4 Qf3+ …

and the same drawing idea is obtained with Qc2, Qd2, Qe2, Qf2.  The

wait

    130 ... Qa4

and in the limit the whole a-file wait

is the same perpetual resource.  The immediate checks Qg2+ and Qh2+

If White tries 131.Kh4 after 130...Qb2, Black can begin checking with ...Qh2+ and then use the h-file/rank to keep the king exposed; the knight on g3 is more of a liability for White than a shield for Black. Qc2 may look tempting because it eyes f5, but the draw does not depend on winning that rook—it depends on maintaining the second-rank/perpetual resource, and Qb2 does that more cleanly while attacking e5.

reflection_text.10:
The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is the classic queen-vs-rook+knight endgame. White king h3, Ng3, Rf5, e5 f4 vs Black Ke8 Qa2. White’s winning idea is Kh4 – Nh5 – e6 with the rook/f-pawn net. Black must keep a perpetual/checking resource and keep the h4 square under control.

The discussion now converges on two essentially equivalent waiting families.

* a-file / third-rank waiting family. Keeping the queen on the a-file keeps the queen out of reach of Rf5/Ng3 and preserves an immediate check on the h-file/rank. The textbook formulation is the waiting/knight-pin 130…Qa3! N, with the same idea written as the a-file stay Qa1 A, Qa4 K, Qa5 J, Qa6 G, Qa7 B, Qa8 I. The most often quoted concrete move in the literature is Qa4, i.e. K, and it is routinely identified with the canonical Qa3 N. From a3/a4 the queen hits the g3-knight, pins the king’s escape to h4 and allows the …Qh3/Qh4/Qg3/Qg4 perpetual shuttle. Colleagues 1,7,10,11,13 etc now explicitly consolidate behind N Qa3 as the precise forcing wait.

* second-rank waiting family. Keeping the queen on the 2nd rank keeps the g2/h2 flight squares covered and the …Qg2+/…Qh2+ perpetual in reserve. The family is Qb2 E, Qc2 L, Qd2 F, Qf2 D. Most colleagues now treat them as transpositional waiting families, with Qa3/Qa4 as the canonical named move and Qb2/Qc2/Qd2 as equivalent practical waits. After 130.Kh3, White’s plan is not only immediate Kh4; he can first improve with Rh5/Nh5/e6 ideas, and the knight on g3 is the piece Black must tie down. 130...Qa3! is the precise move because it attacks that knight along the third rank and keeps the a3–h3 geometry masked by it. If White tries to free the knight, the line opens and Black gets the checking resource; if White ignores it, Black retains the shuttle.

By contrast, Qc2 looks active and even eyes f5, but that is the superficial attraction. It does not address the g3-knight or force White’s hand in the same way. White can save or relocate the rook and continue the Nh5/e6 consolidation without giving Black the same tactical grip. Qb2/Qd2 are similar: they preserve second-rank checks in the abstract, but they do not impose the knight pressure/pin that makes the defense work concretely. That is why I would not fold L into the drawing family.

Qg2/Qh2 lose immediately to Kxg2/Kxh2, Qe2 is met by Nxe2, and Qe6 is the game blunder. Among the listed choices, N: 130...Qa3! remains the textbook drawing resource.

11.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White king is on h3, Ng3 blocks the
3rd rank and Rf5 ties the e pawn.  White’s only winning idea is
Kh4 – e6 – Nh5 and the e6/Nh5 net can be got only if Black gives up
the h4 cover and the g2/h2 checking circuit.

So long as the queen stays in the a-file / 2nd rank corridor the
…Qg2+ / …Qh2+ perpetual can be re-established in one move and
h4 stays covered from the a-file.  That is the whole waiting family.

In a-file form the queen can wait on

Qa1 A, Qa3 N, Qa4 K, Qa5 J, Qa6 G, Qa7 B, Qa8 I

e.g. 130…Qa3! 131 Kh4 Qa4 132 Kh3 Qa3 133 Kh4 … and the same
shuttle is obtained with Qa4, Qa5, Qa6, Qa7, Qa8, Qa1.  The move
normally quoted in the literature is the a-file wait 130…Qa3!
which is the same idea as the commonly written 130…Qa4! K.

In 2nd-rank form the same perpetual is kept by a pure wait on the
second rank which keeps the g2/h2 checks in reserve

Qb2 E, Qc2 L, Qd2 F, Qf2 D

e.g. 130…Qb2 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg4 Qg2+ etc.  Qg2+ C and Qh2+ H
lose the queen at once to Kxg2/Kxh2 and the off-corridor move
130…Qe6, the move actually played, abandons the perpetual and lets
131 Kh4 and the e6/Nh5 net through.

Qe2 M is not a drawing wait in the concrete position: 131 Nxe2 wins
the queen.  That is why the textbook second-rank notation is usually
given as Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qf2 and not as Qe2.

The most precise a-file form is the knight-pin 130…Qa3! N, up to
renaming 130…Qa4! K, the prototype of the a-file/second-rank waiting
family A,B,G,I,J,K,N,E,F,D,L which all draw. ∎

10.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White's only winning try is the King-h4 / Nh5 / e6 net.
As long as the queen stays in the a-file / 2nd rank constellation the
...Qh2+ / ...Qg2+ / ...Qa3+ perpetual can be re-established in one move
and the e6/Nh5 net is never allowed with tempo.

In particular the a-file wait

130...Qa3! N

is the textbook form of the resource.  It is the same idea written as

130...Qa1! A , 130...Qa4! K , 130...Qa5! J , 130...Qa6! G ,
130...Qa7! B , 130...Qa8! I

and up to transposition as the second rank wait

130...Qb2! E , 130...Qc2! L , 130...Qd2! F , 130...Qf2! D

which keeps g2/h2 in reserve and keeps the ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ shuttle alive.
e.g. 130...Qa3 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg5 Qg3+ 133 Kh4 Qh3+... and
130...Qb2 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg5 Qh5+ 133 Kf4 Qf3+... etc.  The Rf8+ 
sacrifice is met by ...Qxf8 on the a3–f8 diagonal.

The checks

130...Qg2+ C 131 Kxg2
130...Qh2+ H 131 Kxh2

lose the queen at once and 130...Qe2 M is 131 Nxe2.  The move actually
played 130...Qe6 abandons the a-file/2nd-rank control, allows 131 Kh4
and the decisive 132 Nh5 e6 net.

The move normally quoted in the literature is the canonical a-file
wait 130...Qa3! N, i.e. in the present list 130...Qa4! K, the prototype of
the whole a-file / second-rank waiting family A,B,D,E,F,G,I,J,K,L,N.
∎

8.text:
After 129.e5 Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the White king is on h3, Ng3 is on g3 and
Rf5 is on f5.  The only way White can get the e6/Nh5 net going is

131.Kh4 132.Nh5

and on the next move e6 with the rook on f5 tied to the defence of e5.
As long as Black can keep the h4 square covered and can restore the
…Qh2+ / …Qg2+ checking circuit in one move the king can never get to
h4.

That is obtained with a pure wait on the a-file or on the 2nd rank.
From the a-file the queen can get to a4 in one move and

…Qa4+  h4

is an immediate checking perpetual.  From the 2nd rank the queen can
get to h2 in one move and

…Qh2+  h3

is the same perpetual.  The two families are transpositional.

* a-file waits
130…Qa1 A, 130…Qa3 N, 130…Qa4 K, 130…Qa5 J, 130…Qa6 G,
130…Qa7 B, 130…Qa8 I

all keep the queen on the a-file, keep the a3–h3 pin on the g3-knight
and give …Qa4+ after any …Kh4.  The move normally quoted in the
literature is the third-rank pin

130…Qa3!

which is the prototype of the whole a-file family, up to renaming
130…Qa4! K.

* 2nd-rank waits
130…Qb2 E, 130…Qc2 L, 130…Qd2 F, 130…Qf2 D

keep the queen on the same rank as the g2/h2 flight squares and keep
…Qh2+ / …Qg2+ in reserve, e.g.

130…Qb2 131.Kh4 Qh2+ 132.Kg5 Qg3+ 133.Kh4 Qh3+ …

The immediate checks

130…Qg2+ C 131.Kxg2
130…Qh2+ H 131.Kxh2

lose the queen at once and

130…Qe2 M

is met on the spot by 131.Nxe2.  The move actually played
130…Qe6 abandons the a-file / 2nd-rank control and allows
131.Kh4 Qh6+ 132.Nh5 with the decisive e6.

In the usual notation the textbook drawing resource is the a-file
wait 130…Qa3! N, the Qa4 K form of the same idea, and the
second-rank form 130…Qb2! E, 130…Qc2 L, 130…Qd2 F, 130…Qf2 D.
That is the whole a-file / 2nd-rank waiting family.

I’ve gone back through the critical geometry after 129...Qa2+ 130.Kh3, and I think the key is more concrete than the broad “a-file/second-rank waiting family” language. The white knight on g3 is not just a blocker; it is the piece that makes White’s Kh4/Nh5/e6 plan work. 130...Qa3! directly attacks and immobilizes it on the third rank while preserving the a-file shuttle. If White tries to continue with Kh4 or e6, Black still has the queen circuit available, and if the knight ever leaves g3, the a3–h3 line opens.

By contrast, Qb2 and Qc2 do keep second-rank checks in reserve, but they leave the knight free. That matters: White can then play Nh5 without the same pin and begin the e6 net; the checks come too late to prevent consolidation. Qc2 especially looks tempting because it eyes f5, but that is a side issue—the rook can move, and Black has not addressed the knight that is shielding the king. Qa4/Qa5 are a-file moves but less precise because they do not hit g3. Qe2 is simply met by Nxe2.

So I’d resist folding all the “waiting” moves into one family. The concrete drawing move to rally around is N, 130...Qa3.

I’m still with **N, 130...Qa3!**. The more I look at the second-rank “family” argument, the more I think it is overgeneralizing. The key is not merely that the queen stays on the second rank; it is that Black must deal with the **Ng3** at the exact moment. After 130.Kh3, White’s freeing idea is Nh5/e6, and the knight on g3 is the piece shielding the king from the a3–h3 line. **130...Qa3!** attacks that knight and keeps the pin geometry alive.

The dangerous alternative is **L, 130...Qc2?**. It looks natural because it eyes the rook on f5, but that is not equivalent. After **130...Qc2 131.Rh5!**, White simply saves the rook and also puts it on the h-file, which blocks some of Black’s checking resources. For example, if Black tries to harass with ...Qg6, White has **132.Kh4**, and now ...Qh6+ is not available in the same way because the white rook on h5 blocks the h-file. The queen on c2 does not attack or tie down Ng3, so White is not prevented from continuing with the e6/Nh5 plan. Immediate ...Qh2+ while the king is still on h3 is just met by Kxh2.

By contrast, **130...Qa3!** keeps the knight under pressure and preserves the precise defensive geometry: if the knight moves, the a3–h3 line opens; if White tries to run with Kh4, Black’s queen has the checking circuit available. I’d treat Qa4/Qb2 as family shorthand, but the cleanest and most forcing drawing resource is the knight-pin move **Qa3**. So I’d consolidate on **N**, and I’d be especially wary of letting Qc2 slip through as “just another second-rank wait.”

is an immediate checking perpetual.  From the 2nd rank the queen can
get to h2 in one move and

…Qh2+  h3

is the same perpetual.  The two families are transpositional.

* a-file waits
130…Qa1 A, 130…Qa3 N, 130…Qa4 K, 130…Qa5 J, 130…Qa6 G,
130…Qa7 B, 130…Qa8 I

all keep the queen on the a-file, keep the a3–h3 pin on the g3-knight
and give …Qa4+ after any …Kh4.  The move normally quoted in the
literature is the third-rank pin

130…Qa3!

which is the prototype of the whole a-file family, up to renaming
130…Qa4! K.

* 2nd-rank waits
130…Qb2 E, 130…Qc2 L, 130…Qd2 F, 130…Qf2 D

keep the queen on the same rank as the g2/h2 flight squares and keep
…Qh2+ / …Qg2+ in reserve, e.g.

130…Qb2 131.Kh4 Qh2+ 132.Kg5 Qg3+ 133.Kh4 Qh3+ …

The immediate checks

130…Qg2+ C 131.Kxg2
130…Qh2+ H 131.Kxh2

lose the queen at once and

130…Qe2 M

is met on the spot by 131.Nxe2.  The move actually played
130…Qe6 abandons the a-file / 2nd-rank control and allows
131.Kh4 Qh6+ 132.Nh5 with the decisive e6.

In the usual notation the textbook drawing resource is the a-file
wait 130…Qa3! N, the Qa4 K form of the same idea, and the
second-rank form 130…Qb2! E, 130…Qc2 L, 130…Qd2 F, 130…Qf2 D.
That is the whole a-file / 2nd-rank waiting family.

is a pure wait on the a-file / 4th rank.  131 Kh4 is now illegal

and the same resource is obtained with any quiet stay of the queen

and with the equivalent pure waits on the 2nd rank

After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the White win is the Kh4–Nh5–e6 net.  The
king can get to h4 iff h4 is not covered and the queen can no longer be
brought back on to the h-file/rank in one move.  The h4 square is covered
from the a file and the g2/h2 perpetual is kept in reserve as long as
the queen stays on the a file or on the 2nd rank.

* 130…Qg2+ 131 Kxg2 and 130…Qh2+ 131 Kxh2 lose the queen at once.
* 130…Qe2 loses at once to 131 Nxe2.

Every pure wait which leaves the queen on the a file or on the 2nd
rank keeps the ...Qa4+ / ...Qh2+ / ...Qg2+ shuttle alive and keeps h4
covered in one move.  Up to transposition the whole waiting family

Qa1 A , Qa3 N , Qa4 K , Qa5 J , Qa6 G , Qa7 B , Qa8 I

and the equivalent 2nd-rank waits

Qb2 E , Qc2 L , Qd2 F , Qf2 D

draws with the perpetual.  The move that is normally quoted in the
literature is the a-file wait

130…Qa4! K

which is the same idea as the text-book 130…Qa3! N and as the second
rank notation 130…Qb2! E, 130…Qc2! L, 130…Qd2! F, 130…Qf2! D.  The
blunder 130…Qe6 abandons the a-file/2nd-rank control and allows

public_text.3:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the whole winning try for White is

131 Kh4 132 Nh5 133 e6

with the f5 rook tied to the defence of e5 and the g3 knight shutting the
3rd rank.  As long as Black can keep the queen in the a-file/second-rank
corridor the h2/g2 checking circuit and the a3–h3 pin can be restored in
one move and the perpetual ...Qg2+/…Qh2+ / …Qa3+ can be kept alive.

The text-book form of the waiting manoeuver is the a-file pin

130… Qa3!

The queen now attacks the g3 knight on the 3rd rank and the a3–h3 line
is masked by that knight.  If White ever tries to move the knight the
a3–h3 line opens and Black has an immediate check, and if White tries to
run the king Black can always return the queen to the 2nd rank in one move
and perpetuate on g2/h2.  Up to renaming the same idea is

Qa1 A , Qa4 K , Qa5 J , Qa6 G , Qa7 B , Qa8 I

and the second-rank form of the same wait

Qb2 E , Qc2 L , Qd2 F , Qf2 D

which keeps the g2/h2 checking circuit in reserve.  The move most often
quoted in the literature is the a-file wait

130… Qa4! K

which is the same perpetual as 130… Qa3! N.  

The immediate checks

130… Qg2+ C 131 Kxg2
130… Qh2+ H 131 Kxh2

lose the queen at once and

130… Qe2 M 131 Nxe2

loses the queen on the spot.  The move actually played 130… Qe6
abandons the a-file/second-rank control, gives White the free tempo
131 Kh4 and the decisive 132 Nh5/e6 net.  This is the a-file/second-rank
waiting family that draws the game, the canonical textbook notation of
which is 130… Qa3! N, essentially the same as 130… Qa4! K.

reflection_text.10:
The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is the classic queen-vs-rook+knight with White K h3, Ng3, Rf5, e5/f4 vs Black Ke8. White’s win is Kh4 – Nh5 – e6 with the f5 rook tied to e5. Black must keep h4 covered and keep a ...Qg2+/...Qh2+ / a3–h3 shuttle in reserve.

Round 2 discussion has coalesced around a waiting constellation.

* a-file waiting family. Keeping the queen on the a-file keeps it out of reach of Rf5/Ng3 and preserves the a3–h3 pin on Ng3 and the ...Qa4+ / ...Qh4+ perpetual after Kh4. The textbook formulation is the knight-pin wait 130...Qa3! N, routinely written as 130...Qa4! K. The same idea is quoted as any quiet stay on the a-file: Qa1 A, Qa3 N, Qa4 K, Qa5 J, Qa6 G, Qa7 B, Qa8 I. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,7,9 now explicitly consolidate behind N Qa3 as the precise forcing wait, with A,B,G,I,J,K as transpositional a-file waits.

* second-rank waiting family. The literature also gives a pure second-rank wait which keeps g2/h2 covered and ...Qh2+/...Qg2+ in reserve: Qb2 E, Qc2 L, Qd2 F, Qf2 D. Colleagues 10,12,2,6,8 maintain the whole family transposes with the a-file family. Colleagues 1,13,14,7,5,9 argue the equivalence is over-generalised: the knight on g3 must be tied down. Qc2 in particular is challenged – after 130...Qc2 131.Rh5! White improves the rook and blocks h-file checking resources, and the move does not attack/pin Ng3 in the same forcing way as Qa3. Qb2/Qd2 are still discussed as plausible second-rank waits, while Qe2 M is repeatedly refuted by 131.Nxe2 and is not a drawing wait. Qf2 is not refuted by Rxf2 because f4 blocks the f-file, but its practical status is less settled than the a-file waits.

Immediate checks are losing: 130...Qg2+ C 131.Kxg2 and 130...Qh2+ H 131.Kxh2 lose the queen at once. The move actually played 130...Qe6 abandons the a-file/second-rank corridor and the a3–f8 diagonal, allowing 131.Kh4 and the decisive Nh5/e6 net.

Unresolved / still debated:
* whether the second-rank waits Qb2/E, Qc2/L, Qd2/F, Qf2/D are formally equivalent to the a-file waits in this concrete pawn structure with e5/f4 blocking a4–h4; the majority of the current round now treats Qa3 as the canonical precise move and is wary of folding Qc2 – and to a lesser extent Qb2/Qd2 – into the drawing family.
* the exact status of Qf2 D vs Qe2 M; consensus is M is lost to Nxe2, D is not materially lost but its drawing force is less championed than the a-file waits.

Current working belief: the drawing resource is the a-file/second-rank waiting constellation, canonically named 130...Qa3! N, up to renaming 130...Qa4! K, with the whole a-file stay A,B,G,I,J,K,N widely quoted as drawing; second-rank waits E,F and arguably L are contested, M is refuted, C and H are immediate losses. The blunder Qe6 is the loss of that geometry.

Qa1 A , Qa3 N , Qa4 K , Qa5 J , Qa6 G , Qa7 B , Qa8 I

The canonical drawing resource is N 130…Qa3! ≈ K 130…Qa4!. reflection_text.12:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White’s winning net is Kh4–Nh5–e6 with Rf5 tied to e5 and Ng3 shutting the 3rd rank. The defence is to keep h4 covered and keep the ...Qg2+ / ...Qh2+ / ...Qa4+ perpetual in reserve. That is the a-file / 2nd-rank waiting corridor.

The key geometry is:
* stay on the a-file so h4 can be covered in one move and the a3–f8 diagonal is kept for a possible ...Qxf8 after Rf8+;
* stay on the 2nd rank so the g2/h2 checking circuit can be restored in one move.

The move actually played 130...Qe6 abandons the corridor, gives 131 Kh4 and the e6/Nh5 net.

Moves that lose immediately:
* 130...Qg2+ C 131 Kxg2, 130...Qh2+ H 131 Kxh2 – queen lost on the spot;
* 130...Qe2 M 131 Nxe2 – the g3 knight takes on e2.

The textbook waiting family is therefore the pure waits that leave the queen on the a-file or on the 2nd rank.

A-file waits, up to transposition:
A Qa1, B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4, N Qa3
all keep the queen on the a-file, keep h4 coverable in one move and keep the a3–h3 pin on Ng3. The canonical notation in the literature is the 3rd-rank pin 130...Qa3! N, normally written as the a-file wait 130...Qa4! K.

Second-rank waits that keep the g2/h2 circuit in reserve:
E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, D Qf2
e.g. 130...Qb2 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg5 Qg3+ etc. The same perpetual is obtainable from c2/d2/f2. Qe2 is not part of the family in the concrete position.

Disagreement in the room: Colleagues 1,13,7 argue for a single precise move, 130...Qa3! N, because it directly attacks Ng3 and ties the knight down, and they are wary of over-generalising the whole second-rank family, e.g. Qc2 L allowing Rh5 and reducing the knight pressure. 1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m still with **N, 130...Qa3!**. The main thing this round should settle is that “a-file/second-rank waiting family” is too broad for a single-choice question. Several moves keep *some* checking resource, but the drawing move has to address White’s concrete consolidation after **130.Kh3**, namely **Kh4/Nh5/e6** with **Ng3** shielding the king.

**130...Qa3!** is the precise form because it attacks/tethers the **g3-knight** on the third rank while preserving the a-file geometry. If White tries to free the knight or continue with the h4 plan, Black’s queen has the right checking circuit and the a3–f8 diagonal remains covered against a timely **Rf8+** resource.

The dangerous trap is **L, 130...Qc2**. It looks natural because it eyes **f5**, but that does not attack or pin **Ng3**. White is not forced to save the rook immediately; the important plan is the king/knight/pawn net, and Qc2 does not restrain it in the same way. In a single-answer setting, that is exactly the kind of “second-rank wait” that gets overincluded by the family argument.

**Qa4/K** and **Qb2/E** are closer family forms, but they are less precise than the immediate knight-pressure move. **Qg2/Qh2** lose instantly to **Kxg2/Kxh2**, **Qe2** is met by **Nxe2**, and **Qe6** was the game blunder because it abandoned this control. So I’d consolidate on **N: 130...Qa3!**.

9.text:

The tempting alternative **L, 130...Qc2**, keeps some second-rank checking motifs, but it does not attack or restrain Ng3. That matters because White gets a free move to improve the rook and continue the Nh5/e6 consolidation; the checks come too late. Also, Qc2 abandons the a3–f8 diagonal, so a later Rf8+ resource is not met as cleanly as with the queen on a3.

Qa4/K and Qb2/E are closer in spirit, but they are not the same forcing blow. Qa4 covers h4 but does not hit g3; Qb2 keeps checks in reserve but leaves the knight unpinned. In a single-best-answer setting, the precise drawing resource is the third-rank knight-pin **130...Qa3!**, with the a-file shuttle still available if White tries Kh4. After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 White's only way to get the e6/Nh5 net going is

131 Kh4 132 Nh5 133 e6

with Rf5 tied to the defence of e5 and Ng3 shutting the 3rd rank.  As long
as Black can keep h4 covered in one move and can restore the
...Qg2+/...Qh2+/...Qa4+ shuttle in one move the king can never get to
h4.  That is the a-file / 2nd-rank waiting constellation.

The checks

130...Qg2+ C 131 Kxg2
130...Qh2+ H 131 Kxh2

lose the queen on the spot and 130...Qe2 M is 131 Nxe2.  The move actually
played 130...Qe6 abandons the corridor and allows 131 Kh4 and the
decisive Nh5/e6 net.

Any pure wait which leaves the queen on the a-file keeps the a3–h3/a4–h4
geometry alive and the ...Qa4+ perpetual in reserve after a ...Kh4,
e.g.

130...Qa1 A , 130...Qa3 N , 130...Qa4 K , 130...Qa5 J ,
130...Qa6 G , 130...Qa7 B , 130...Qa8 I

and any pure wait which leaves the queen on the 2nd rank keeps the
g2/h2 checking circuit in reserve, e.g.

130...Qb2 E , 130...Qd2 F , 130...Qf2 D

130...Qc2 L is transpositional with the same 2nd-rank wait.  
For instance

130...Qa3! 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg5 Qg3+ 133 Kh4 Qh3+ …
130...Qa4! 131 Kh4 Qa3 132 Kh3 Qa4 133 Kh4 …

and with the second-rank form

130...Qb2 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg5 Qh5+ 133 Kf4 Qf3+ …

The Rf8+ sacrifice is met by …Qxf8 on the a3–f8 diagonal and the e6
/ Nh5 net is never allowed with tempo because h4 stays covered and
the checking circuit can be restored in one move.

In the literature the resource is normally quoted in the knight-pin
form

130...Qa3! N

i.e. up to notation 130...Qa4! K, the prototype of the whole
a-file/second-rank waiting family A,B,G,I,J,K,N,E,F,D,L which all draw.

I’m still with **N, 130...Qa3!**. The main thing this round should settle is that “a-file/second-rank waiting family” is too broad for a single-choice question. Several moves keep *some* checking resource, but the drawing move has to address White’s concrete consolidation after **130.Kh3**, namely **Kh4/Nh5/e6** with **Ng3** shielding the king.

**130...Qa3!** is the precise form because it attacks/tethers the **g3-knight** on the third rank while preserving the a-file geometry. If White tries to free the knight or continue with the h4 plan, Black’s queen has the right checking circuit and the a3–f8 diagonal remains covered against a timely **Rf8+** resource.

The dangerous trap is **L, 130...Qc2**. It looks natural because it eyes **f5**, but that does not attack or pin **Ng3**. White is not forced to save the rook immediately; the important plan is the king/knight/pawn net, and Qc2 does not restrain it in the same way. In a single-answer setting, that is exactly the kind of “second-rank wait” that gets overincluded by the family argument.

**Qa4/K** and **Qb2/E** are closer family forms, but they are less precise than the immediate knight-pressure move. **Qg2/Qh2** lose instantly to **Kxg2/Kxh2**, **Qe2** is met by **Nxe2**, and **Qe6** was the game blunder because it abandoned this control. So I’d consolidate on **N: 130...Qa3!**.

reflection_text.11:
The position after 129...Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kh3 Ng3 Rf5 e5/f4 vs Black Ke8. White's win is Kh4 → Nh5 → e6 with Rf5 tied to e5 and Ng3 shutting the 3rd rank. The defence is a pure wait that keeps h4 covered in one move and keeps the ...Qg2+/...Qh2+/...Qa4+ perpetual in reserve in one move. Immediate checks lose: 130...Qg2+ C 131 Kxg2, 130...Qh2+ H 131 Kxh2, and 130...Qe2 M is 131 Nxe2. 130...Qe6 is the game blunder that abandons the a-file/2nd-rank corridor and lets 131 Kh4 through.

The drawing constellation is the a-file/second-rank wait. In a-file form the queen can stay on Qa1 A, Qa3 N, Qa4 K, Qa5 J, Qa6 G, Qa7 B, Qa8 I, keeping the a3–h3 / a4–h4 geometry and the a3–f8 ...Qxf8 resource. The canonical forcing form of the idea is the third-rank pin 130...Qa3! N, i.e. up to notation 130...Qa4! K, which attacks/tethers Ng3 and masks a3–h3. If White tries Kh4 Black restores Qa4+/Qh2+/Qg2+ perpetuals, e.g. 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kg5 Qg4+ etc.

In second-rank form the same perpetual is kept by a pure wait on the 2nd rank which keeps the g2/h2 checking circuit in reserve: Qb2 E, Qd2 F, Qf2 D, e.g. 130...Qb2 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg5 Qg3+ etc. Qc2 L is now repeatedly flagged as the weak member of the second-rank family: it stays on the 2nd rank but does not hit/restrain Ng3, so White can improve with 131 Rh5! and continue the Nh5/e6 consolidation with tempo, and it is distinguished from the knight-pin Qa3.

Current round consensus is narrowing to the precise knight-pressure move 130...Qa3! N as the single best-answer canonical resource, with 130...Qa4! K as its usual textbook renaming. The a-file family A,B,G,I,J,K,N is widely accepted as drawing up to transposition; the second-rank core E,F,D is accepted by the family view, while Qc2 L is disputed and is increasingly treated as not equivalent. Qe2 M, Qg2+ C, Qh2+ H and the played Qe6 remain losing.

Unresolved: exact engine preference between a-file wait vs second-rank wait, and whether Qf2 D is strictly equivalent to Qb2 E given the e-file opening. The invariant that survives is: stay on the a-file/second-rank corridor, avoid immediate checks and off-corridor moves like Qe6/Qe2.

reflection_text.4:
Position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3. White’s only practical winning net is 131 Kh4 132 Nh5 133 e6 with Rf5 tied to the defence of e5 and Ng3 shutting the 3rd rank. The king can get to h4 iff h4 is not covered in one move and the …Qg2+ / …Qh2+ checking shuttle can no longer be restored in one move. The drawing constellation is therefore the a-file / 2nd-rank wait which keeps h4 covered and keeps the g2/h2 checking circuit in reserve in one move.

The forcing canonical form of the resource is the third-rank pin on the g3-knight:

130…Qa3! N

Qa3 attacks/tethers Ng3 on the 3rd rank, masks the a3–h3 line and keeps the a-file geometry for a …Qa4+ perpetual after any …Kh4, e.g. 131 Kh4 Qa4+ 132 Kg5 Qg4+ 133 Kh5 Qh4+… The …Rf8+ sacrifice is met by …Qxf8 on the a3–f8 diagonal and the e6/Nh5 net is never allowed with tempo. Up to renaming this is the textbook a-file wait 130…Qa4! K.

Whole a-file stay up to transposition:
Qa1 A , Qa3 N , Qa4 K , Qa5 J , Qa6 G , Qa7 B , Qa8 I
all keep the queen on the a-file, keep the a3–f8 diagonal for …Qxf8 and allow h4 to be covered next move.

Up to transposition the same perpetual is kept by a pure wait on the second rank which keeps the g2/h2 checking circuit in reserve:
Qb2 E , Qd2 F , Qf2 D
e.g. 130…Qb2 131 Kh4 Qh2+ 132 Kg5 Qg3+ 133 Kh4 Qh3+…

Immediate checks are refuted on the spot:
130…Qg2+ C 131 Kxg2
130…Qh2+ H 131 Kxh2
130…Qe2 M is 131 Nxe2 because Ng3 covers e2. The move actually played 130…Qe6 abandons the a-file/2nd-rank corridor, lets 131 Kh4 through and allows the decisive Nh5/e6 net.

Current round sharpened the family vs precise distinction. Qa3 is the precise move that puts immediate pressure on Ng3 while preserving the a-file geometry and the …Qh2+/…Qg2+ shuttle. Qa4 is the same idea written as the textbook a-file wait and is transpositional with the a-file stays. Qb2/Qd2/Qf2 keep checking motifs but are less forcing than the knight-pin. Qc2 L is the disputed marginal member of the second-rank family: it does not hit/restrain Ng3 and in the concrete line White has the improving 131 Rh5! which changes the tempo of the checking shuttle, so colleagues now consistently exclude it from the single-best-answer set.

Consensus in round 4 converges on the canonical precise drawing resource 130…Qa3! N ≈ 130…Qa4! K, the prototype of the a-file/second-rank waiting family A,B,G,I,J,K,N and, up to transposition, E,F,D. Qg2+, Qh2+, Qe2 and the played Qe6 are losing. Unresolved tension remains about the exact equivalence of the peripheral a-file squares Qa1/Qa5/Qa6/Qa7/Qa8 and about the status of Qc2; the prevailing judgment is that Qa3/Qa4 is the cleanest single-best answer.
